kepler.name: Johannes Kepler
kepler.bio: Provincial Mathematician at Graz (1594–1600), Imperial Mathematician to Rudolph II at Prague (1601–1612), and Mathematician at Linz (1612–1626). Author of Prodromus Dissertationum Cosmographicarum continens Mysterium Cosmographicum (1596/1621), Astronomia Nova (1609), Strena seu de Nive Sexangula (1611), and Harmonices Mundi Libri V (1619). Unified Copernican heliocentrism with Euclidean regular solids, formulated the Kepler Right Triangle (1, √φ, φ), posed the sphere close-packing Kepler Conjecture, discovered the rhombic dodecahedron, rhombic triacontahedron, and stellated dodecahedra, proved the complete classification of the 11 uniform planar tilings and 13 Archimedean solids, analyzed the algebraic non-constructibility of the regular heptagon, and discovered the three laws of planetary motion.

maestlin.name: Michael Mästlin
maestlin.role: German Astronomer & Professor of Mathematics at Tübingen
maestlin.bio: Kepler's revered teacher at the University of Tübingen who introduced him to Copernican astronomy, oversaw the printing of the 1596 Tübingen edition of Mysterium Cosmographicum (appending Rheticus's Narratio Prima and calculating planetary distances), and corresponded with Kepler in October 1597 on the Kepler Right Triangle (1, √φ, φ), computing the first known decimal approximation of 1/φ ≈ 0.6180340.

copernicus.name: Nicolaus Copernicus
copernicus.bio: Author of De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1543), whose heliocentric ordering of the six mobile planetary orbs (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Earth, Venus, Mercury) supplied the empirical astronomical framework for Kepler's five-polyhedron cosmological hypothesis in Mysterium Cosmographicum.

brahe.name: Tycho Brahe
brahe.bio: Master of Uraniborg whose unprecedentedly accurate naked-eye planetary observations—especially of Mars's eccentricity—compelled Kepler to refine circular Copernican orbs into focal ellipses (Astronomia Nova, 1609) and revealed the exact extremal angular velocities governed by harmonic ratios in Harmonices Mundi Book V (1619).

euclid.name: Euclid of Alexandria
euclid.role: Greek Geometer, Author of the Stoicheia (Elements)
euclid.bio: Kepler's supreme mathematical authority throughout Mysterium Cosmographicum and Harmonices Mundi: Books II (Prop. 11), IV (Props. 10–16), X (classification of incommensurable binomials, apotomes, and medial magnitudes), and XIII (construction of the five regular solids and proof in XIII.18 that no sixth regular convex polyhedron can exist) form the demonstrative backbone of Kepler's geometry.

proclus.name: Proclus Diadochus
proclus.bio: Head of the Athenian Academy and author of the Commentary on the First Book of Euclid's Elements, quoted extensively in Greek and Latin by Kepler in Harmonices Mundi Books I and IV to ground geometric knowability (scibilitas) and innate archetypal harmony in the human mind.

pythagoras.name: Pythagoras of Samos
pythagoras.role: Greek Philosopher, Geometer & Theorist of Cosmic Harmony
pythagoras.bio: Founder of the Pythagorean tradition linking integer musical consonances, the pentagram (stella quinquangula), cosmic harmony, and the right-triangle theorem (Euclid I.47)—celebrated by Kepler alongside the Divine Section as the first of the 'two great treasures of geometry'.

plato.name: Plato of Athens
plato.role: Greek Philosopher, Founder of the Academy
plato.bio: Author of the Timaeus, which associated four regular polyhedra with the elemental bodies and the dodecahedron with the cosmos as a whole; honored by Kepler as precursor to the polyhedral archetype of creation.

aristotle.name: Aristotle of Stagira
aristotle.bio: Author of Posterior Analytics, De Caelo, and Metaphysics. Kepler critically engages Aristotle's denial of mathematical causality in physics and refutes the ancient claim that regular tetrahedra tile three-dimensional space without gaps.

archimedes.name: Archimedes of Syracuse
archimedes.bio: Discoverer of the thirteen semi-regular convex polyhedra originally recorded by Pappus in Synagoge Book V; Kepler was the first modern mathematician to reconstruct, name, and rigorously prove the completeness of all thirteen Archimedean solids in Harmonices Mundi Book II.

pappus.name: Pappus of Alexandria
pappus.bio: Author of the Mathematical Collection (Synagoge), whose Book V preserved the face counts of the thirteen Archimedean semi-regular polyhedra and analyzed the hexagonal economy of bees' honeycombs—extended by Kepler into three dimensions in Strena (1611) and Harmonices Mundi Book II (1619).

apollonius.name: Apollonius of Perga
apollonius.role: Greek Geometer, Author of the Conics
apollonius.bio: The 'Great Geometer' whose Conica provided the exact focal and projective theory of the ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola applied by Kepler to planetary orbits and solid geometric problems.

ptolemy.name: Claudius Ptolemy
ptolemy.bio: Author of the Almagest (whose chord calculation for the pentagon and decagon in Book I.10 is cited by Kepler) and the Harmonics (three books), which Kepler analyzed and compared with his own celestial harmonies in the Appendix to Harmonices Mundi.

campanus.name: Campanus of Novara
campanus.role: Italian Medieval Mathematician & Commentator on Euclid
campanus.bio: Editor of the Latin Elementa (printed Venice 1482), noted for studying the star pentagram's angle sum and irrational ratios in Euclid Book X.

fibonacci.name: Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci)
fibonacci.bio: Author of Liber Abaci (1202) and Practica Geometriae (1220). In Strena (1611), Kepler independently formulated the self-generating additive law 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21... and demonstrated that successive ratios converge to Euclid's extreme and mean ratio (φ), connecting botanical pentamery to phyllotaxis.

pacioli.name: Fra Luca Bartolomeo de Pacioli
pacioli.bio: Author of De Divina Proportione (Venice, 1509, with polyhedral illustrations by Leonardo da Vinci), establishing the Renaissance terminology of the 'Divine Proportion' (sectio divina) that Kepler elevated to a generative law of geometry, botany, and celestial architecture.

duerer.name: Albrecht Dürer
duerer.bio: Author of Underweysung der Messung mit dem Zirckel und Richtscheyt (Nuremberg, 1525), pioneering unfolded planar polyhedral nets, approximate heptagon constructions, and pentagonal tilings studied and corrected by Kepler.

ramus.name: Petrus Ramus (Pierre de la Ramée)
ramus.role: French Humanist Logician & Critic of Euclid
ramus.bio: Author of Scholae Mathematicae (1569), who dismissed Euclid's Book X on incommensurables as an obscure and useless labyrinth; forcefully refuted by Kepler in Harmonices Mundi Book I Prooemium once Kepler discovered that Book X's degrees of rationality govern constructible harmonic polygons.

snellius.name: Willebrord Snellius
snellius.bio: Professor of Mathematics at Leiden who echoed Ramus's skepticism regarding Euclid Book X; gently answered by Kepler in Harmonices Mundi Book I to show that Euclid's classification of binomials and apotomes separates knowable plane figures from unknowable ones.

buergi.name: Jost Bürgi
buergi.role: Swiss Imperial Clockmaker, Instrument Maker & Algebraist
buergi.bio: Imperial Kammeruhrmacher in Prague and Kassel, co-inventor of logarithms, and author of the Cossic algebraic chord equation for the regular heptagon and nonagon—cited and analyzed critically by Kepler in Harmonices Mundi Book I Props. XLV–XLVII to distinguish algebraic root-finding from Euclidean geometric constructibility.

wackher.name: Johannes Matthäus Wackher von Wackenfels
wackher.role: Imperial Aulic Councillor & Humanist Patron in Prague
wackher.bio: Kepler's learned friend and dedicatee of Strena seu de Nive Sexangula (1611), whose love of paradoxical natural philosophy inspired Kepler's New Year's gift investigating why snowflakes always fall with sixfold symmetry.

galileo.name: Galileo Galilei
galileo.bio: Correspondent of Kepler since receiving Mysterium Cosmographicum in 1597; discoverer of Jupiter's four Medicean moons (Sidereus Nuncius, 1610), defended by Kepler in Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo (1610) and incorporated into Harmonices Mundi Book V.

frisch.name: Christian Frisch
frisch.role: German Philologist & Editor of Kepler's Opera Omnia
frisch.bio: Editor of the monumental eight-volume Joannis Kepleri Astronomi Opera Omnia (Frankfurt & Erlangen, 1858–1871), preserving critical Public Domain editions of Mysterium Cosmographicum (1596/1621), Kepler's correspondence with Mästlin, Strena (1611), and Harmonices Mundi (1619).

poinsot.name: Louis Poinsot
poinsot.bio: Rediscovered Kepler's small and great stellated dodecahedra in 1809 along with their duals (the great dodecahedron and great icosahedron), completing the four regular non-convex Kepler–Poinsot star polyhedra.

gauss.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
gauss.bio: Proved in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801, §365–366) that a regular n-gon is constructible by ruler and compass if and only if odd prime factors of n are distinct Fermat primes (3, 5, 17, 257, 65537), vindicating Kepler's 1619 non-constructibility thesis for the regular 7-gon, 9-gon, 11-gon, and 13-gon while revealing the unexpected constructibility of the 17-gon.

wantzel.name: Pierre Laurent Wantzel
wantzel.bio: Published the first complete algebraic proof in 1837 that irreducible cubic equations—and hence angle trisection, cube duplication, and the regular heptagon and nonagon—cannot be solved in quadratic radical towers (ruler-and-compass extensions), formalizing Kepler's 1619 degree-obstruction argument.

thompson.name: Sir D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson
thompson.bio: Author of On Growth and Form (1917/1942), extending Kepler's Strena (1611) analysis of close-packed spheres, honeycomb trihedral maraldi angles, rhombic dodecahedra, and botanical phyllotaxis into modern mathematical morphology.

penrose.name: Sir Roger Penrose
penrose.bio: Discovered non-periodic fivefold planar tilings (1974) directly inspired by Kepler's pentagonal and decagonal star tessellation (Figure Aa) in Harmonices Mundi Book II (1619), foreshadowing physical icosahedral quasicrystals.

coxeter.name: Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter
coxeter.bio: Author of Regular Polytopes (1948) and Introduction to Geometry (1961), who systematized Kepler's Schläfli-type vertex classifications of uniform tilings, Archimedean solids, stellated polyhedra, and golden zonohedra.

hoenen.name: Petrus Hubertus Jacobus Hoenen, S.J.
hoenen.role: Dutch Jesuit Physicist & Philosopher of Mathematics
hoenen.bio: Author of De Noetica Geometriae (1954), investigating intelligible geometric extension and exact necessity across the Euclidean and modern mathematical traditions in the GEOMETOR Digital Scriptorium.

cusanus.name: Nicolaus Cusanus (Nicholas of Cusa)
cusanus.bio: Author of De Docta Ignorantia (1440) and De Mathematicis Complementis; praised by Kepler as 'divinus mihi Cusanus' in Mysterium Cosmographicum Caput II for contrasting the curved (sphere, archetype of the Divine Trinity) with the straight (inscribed polyhedra, archetype of the created world).

rheticus.name: Georg Joachim Rheticus
rheticus.bio: Author of the Narratio Prima (1540), the first published account of Copernicus's heliocentric system, which Michael Mästlin reprinted directly alongside Kepler's 1596 editio princeps of Mysterium Cosmographicum.

hales.name: Thomas Callister Hales
hales.bio: Proved the 1611 Kepler Sphere-Packing Conjecture in 1998 (published 2005) and completed its machine-checked formal verification in the Flyspeck project (2014), confirming that no packing of congruent spheres in Euclidean 3-space exceeds π/(3√2) ≈ 74.048%.
